title: PhysMetrics.Weather: An Evaluation Framework for Physical Consistency in ML Weather Models
claim: A multi-part evaluation suite is organized into metric families, each probing a distinct physical property of model outputs.
layout: 7 panels in a grid around a central globe, color-coded by metric type
description: A dense poster-like figure with seven rectangular panels (A–G) arranged around a central photo of the Earth. Panels are color-coded: blue for conservation (dry air mass, water mass, total energy), beige for spectral energy distribution, and olive green for dynamical balance (geostrophic, hydrostatic, thermodynamic stability). Each panel has a bold title with its metric symbol (δd, δW, δε, E(k), RMSE, W1), a lettered badge, and a small illustration. The illustrations include an atmospheric column, energy icons, an energy-spectrum plot, balance scales, a weather map, and a lapse-rate wedge. Each panel also shows the key equation. A caption bar at the bottom of each panel states in plain language what it measures. Thin lines link the panels to the globe in the center, which is the visual focus.
caption: Overview of PhysMetrics.Weather. PhysMetrics.Weather evaluates models using nine metrics across three metric types: conservation of mass and energy (blue), spectral energy distribution (beige), and adherence to dynamical balance (green). Metric definitions are detailed in Table [ref]. A. Dry Air Mass Conservation: tracks global dry air mass. B. Global Water Mass Consistency: tracks the atmospheric water budget. C. Total Energy Consistency: estimates the global energy budget across sensible, potential, latent, and kinetic states. D. Spectral Energy Distribution: evaluates the spectral distribution of wind energy across spatial frequencies (using three metrics). E. Geostrophic RMSE: evaluates if models reproduce the relationship between wind speeds and pressure gradients (the Coriolis effect). F. Hydrostatic RMSE: evaluates atmospheric stability by checking the temperature of the air between two pressure levels. G. Thermodynamic Stability: evaluates the plausibility of vertical temperature gradients (lapse rates) across climate zones.
abstract: Machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models have achieved impressive forecasting performance at a small fraction of the computational costs required for traditional physics-based methods. However, they are primarily (1) data-driven and (2) evaluated using pixel-wide error metrics (e.g., RMSE), so there are no guarantees that their forecasts are consistent with known physical laws. We introduce PhysMetrics$.$Weather, an evaluation framework that assesses the physical realism of MLWP models across three types of metrics: conservation, spectral, and dynamical. By quantifying physical realism, this tool guides the development of physics-informed architectures and helps evaluate whether MLWP models are reliable for operational use. Our framework is available on Github at https://github.com/Emmakast/PhysMetrics.Weather.
